items.paragraph: (Download the transcript below)

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph:
OK, so, you’re responsible for your area. The buck stops with you. You have accountability. You have ownership. Now, how do you take responsibility for all the moving parts without micromanaging the details?

If you’re going to be responsible for everything, you have to make sure everything is running smoothly. If you’re going to be responsible for making sure everything is running smoothly, you need to be involved in the details, right? I mean, how can you ensure a successful outcome if you don’t know everything that’s going on?

Not so fast…

items.title: CONTINUE
items.completeHint: Complete the content above before moving on.

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph:
The truth is, some leaders — well-meaning leaders — get this far into understanding responsibility and ownership and then get stuck. Their extreme sense of responsibility spills over into the dreaded world of micromanaging.

Click on each circle in the illustration below for examples of micromanaging.

items.description: Sitting in on every new hire interview

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph:
Maybe this rings a bell with you or someone you know. After all, that’s unconditional ownership, right?

Not necessarily.

items.date: Now, depending on the size of your company, some of this may be necessary.
items.description: If you have a company of 10 people total, maybe some of these responsibilities do fall on you. Chances are, though, you’re not in that category. Or maybe you started in that category and grew out of it long ago, but you’re still operating like you’re a one-person band.

items.date: All jokes aside, not only is all of the above exhausting … it’s unscalable. You could do it for a very short season, but before long, the weight will start to crush you.
items.description: And know what’s worse? It starts to crush those you lead. With your fingers in every pie, the team never learns how to cook, metaphorically speaking. People either gravitate toward two areas: They don’t think for themselves (why would they, if you’re going to wind up making every decision for the group?) or they’re so terrified to make a mistake they can’t do anything without approval. They default to order-takers, and any unique characteristics or skills you hired them for in the first place get buried.

items.date: Not only that, but being overextended takes away from other more important duties you may have, like keeping your department in the black, outlining your vision, working on the hiring plan, or opening a new branch.
items.description:
If your time had a dollar amount of what you’re worth to the company (not your literal hourly wage, but the amount of money your decisions bring in per month), would the best use of your time be researching costs for a new type of coffee in the break room or rewriting the second paragraph of the company newsletter? What about sitting in four meetings each week about processes and procedures? Deciding whether a button on a website will be green or blue? What picture should go in the new brochure?

Probably none of the above. There are certain things that only you can do, and it’s most important to make time for those.

items.heading: Exercise
items.paragraph:
Which of these is an unintended outcome of micromanaging?

Drag and drop each card to complete this element.

items.title: It takes your time away from other more important duties.
Your team learns to do things on their own.
It starts to crush those you lead.
It’s unscalable.
Your team won’t learn to think for themselves.
Your team will be terrified to make mistakes.
The team becomes order-takers.
The team will be hesitant to do anything without approval.
Your teammates learn when to consult you and when to take risks.
Team members like it.
You will have more free time in your day.
CONTINUE
items.completeHint: Complete the content above before moving on.

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph:
When leaders realize that wearing themselves out over details like the above is not only making them tired, but squashing their team, it can be a freeing revelation.

So, how do you hold yourself responsible for all the things that can go right or wrong without being involved in the day-to-day operations?

Part of it goes back to the classic definition of leadership. You may have heard it before:

You manage things, and you lead people.

The people as a team do the thing, whether it’s running a company or winning a national championship, and you lead them to do it well, like Pat did. Their achievement is your achievement, the team’s achievement, so you train them to do it well. Then get out of the way.

That’s it. That doesn’t mean you don’t step in in an emergency. That doesn’t mean you’re always in the dark. You don’t do it for them, you don’t do it with them. You hire smart people, people who are a good fit, and make sure they have what they need to do their job well.

items.title: CONTINUE
items.completeHint: Complete the content above before moving on.

items.paragraph: Understanding the importance of being “hands off” is one of the most fundamental (and often overlooked) tenets of good leadership.

Sometimes as a leader, we think our strength lies in getting the team to produce a certain level of output — after all, it’s what we’re all responsible for. You may even be tempted to jump in and help them. But at the end of the day, you can’t make people do things. You have to lead them. All you can really do is hire well.

We’ll say it again. All you can really do is get the right people in the right seat on the bus and lead them well to do their jobs. You can’t force them to do it with excellence, innovation, positivity, super-service, or creativity. All you can do is fire them if they don’t and replace them with someone else who will. Then the cycle starts again.

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph:
As the leader, you have to lead them in attitude, vision, excellence, motivation — all the principles Pat championed in the Definite Dozen — guiding them to the level of self-discipline, autonomy, or ingenuity you want.

They will know what that level is because it will be modeled by you. Not done by you on behalf of the team or for the team but encouraged by the level of leadership you provide.

Which of these is an example of being “hands-off” vs “hands-on”?

Drag and drop each card to complete this element.

items.title: Letting team members experiment with new methods
Daily status meetings
Focusing on results, not minute-by-minute activity
Not needing to approve every small decision
Overseeing each step of a project
Excessive reporting
Encouraging problem-solving
Dictating how to do things
CONTINUE
items.completeHint: Complete the content above before moving on.

items.paragraph: (Download the transcript below)

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph: Listen to Sr. Vice President Petra Dunn of Merrill Lynch Wealth Management remember how she learned to delegate and become more “hands off” in her early career.

Which of the following is an example of micromanaging vs. macromanaging?

Drag and drop each card to complete this element.

items.title: Approving minor updates to the website
Asking for a monthly update report from your team
Showing the writing team how to write articles
Picking out the wine options for an incentive lunch
Having your employees keep an hourly log
Approving major product initiatives
Making sure the team knows that without you, they'd be lost
Stepping in to take over a project when a team member stumbles
Leading a quarterly meeting for your team
Being copied on the test send of every outgoing email
Outlining the one-, five-, and 10-year vision for your area
Making sure all ideas for the product come from you
Having an open-door policy
Hosting an offsite retreat for your team members
Making a note of the time the admin spends away from their desk
Overtaking the new-hire training to make sure it’s done "right"
Asking the finance team to cc you on every invoice, no matter how small
Having one-on-ones with team members you manage
CONTINUE

lessons.title: Knowledge Check

items.title: Micromanaging is_________________.

answers.title: The desire to control every part, however small, of an enterprise or activity.
Caring about the quality of your team’s work.
Training team members to have attention to the detail.

items.title: Which of these is an example of micromanaging?

answers.title: Setting clear goals for the team
Asking your admin to automatically include you on every department meeting
Asking for quarterly progress reports
Letting your team present new ideas

items.title: What are some of the disadvantages of micromanaging as a leader?

answers.title: It’s not scalable.
Your team won’t learn to think for themselves.
All of the above.

items.paragraph: Refer to your workbook for the reflection questions below.
On a scale of 1 to 10, how much do you micromanage vs. macromanage?

In what particular areas might you be exerting too much control?

Why? What is the fear?
Is there anyone on your team who could be entrusted with more responsibility?
Are there any areas that might need more leadership oversight?

Sources:
